name: Electron (size upper limit)
blurb: Electrons behave as point particles, so no true size has been measured. Experiments set only an upper limit of about 10⁻¹⁸ metres.

howWeKnow.text: Collisions between electrons and other particles show no internal structure down to about 10⁻¹⁸ m, which gives only an upper limit on its size.

name: Neutron
blurb: A neutron is a particle found in atomic nuclei. It is about 1.6 femtometres across, tens of thousands of times smaller than an atom.

howWeKnow.text: Scattering experiments fire particles at neutrons and measure how they spread out, giving a size of roughly 1.6 femtometres; the value is approximate.

name: Uranium-238 nucleus
blurb: The nucleus of uranium-238, the most common uranium isotope, is about 15 femtometres across. It holds 92 protons and 146 neutrons.

howWeKnow.text: Electrons fired at the nucleus are deflected by its charge spread, and the pattern gives a radius of about 7 femtometres.

name: Electron Compton wavelength
blurb: A length calculated from the electron's mass, Planck's constant and the speed of light. Below this scale, quantum effects of electrons dominate.

howWeKnow.text: Planck's constant divided by the electron's mass times the speed of light gives about 2.43 picometres.

name: Hydrogen atom
blurb: Hydrogen is the simplest atom, with one proton and one electron. The atom is about 0.1 nanometres across, set by where the electron is likely to be.

howWeKnow.text: Solving the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen gives a Bohr radius of about 0.053 nanometres, so the atom is about twice that across.

name: Iron atom
blurb: Iron atoms in solid metal pack together like tiny spheres. Each is about a quarter of a nanometre across.

howWeKnow.text: X-ray patterns from iron crystals reveal the spacing between atoms, giving an atomic radius of roughly 126 picometres.

name: Water molecule
blurb: A water molecule is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms at an angle of about 105 degrees. It is roughly 0.28 nanometres across.

howWeKnow.text: Microwave spectra reveal bond lengths and angles, from which the overall molecular size of about 0.28 nanometres is calculated.

name: Caesium atom
blurb: Caesium is one of the largest stable atoms. Its outer electron sits far from the nucleus, which is why it is used in atomic clocks.

howWeKnow.text: The metallic radius of caesium, about 265 picometres, is found from X-ray crystal patterns, giving a diameter near 0.53 nanometres.

name: Glucose molecule
blurb: Glucose is a simple sugar that cells use for energy. The molecule is roughly 0.7 nanometres across, depending on how it is oriented.

howWeKnow.text: Crystal structures give atomic positions, and modelling the bond geometry gives an approximate overall size of 0.7 nanometres.

name: Buckminsterfullerene (buckyball)
blurb: Buckminsterfullerene is a cage of 60 carbon atoms shaped like a football. The cage is about 0.7 nanometres across.

howWeKnow.text: X-ray crystallography of solid samples gives a cage diameter of about 0.71 nanometres between the centres of opposite atoms.

name: Haemoglobin
blurb: Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The molecule is about 6 nanometres across.

howWeKnow.text: Crystal structures of haemoglobin, first solved in the 1960s, show a molecule roughly 6.4 by 5.5 nanometres in size.

name: Ribosome
blurb: Ribosomes are molecular machines that build proteins by following instructions carried in RNA. They are about 25 nanometres across, too small for light microscopes.

howWeKnow.text: Cryo-electron microscopy of frozen ribosomes gives their three-dimensional shape, which measures roughly 20 to 30 nanometres across.

name: HIV virus
blurb: HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, is a roughly spherical particle about 120 nanometres across. Light microscopes cannot resolve it.

howWeKnow.text: Electron microscope images of purified virus particles show diameters of about 120 nanometres, varying a little between particles.

name: Green light (wavelength)
blurb: Visible light is a wave with wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometres. Green light sits near 550 nanometres, where human eyes are most sensitive.

howWeKnow.text: A diffraction grating splits white light into colours, and measuring the angle of each colour gives its wavelength, about 550 nanometres for green.

name: E. coli bacterium
blurb: Escherichia coli is a rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the guts of humans and other animals. A typical cell is about 2 micrometres long.

howWeKnow.text: Microscopes measure the length of cultured cells, which typically falls around 2 micrometres.

name: Red blood cell
blurb: Red blood cells are flexible discs that carry oxygen around the body. Each is about 7 micrometres across and squeezes through capillaries narrower than itself.

howWeKnow.text: Measured on stained blood smears under a microscope, healthy adult red blood cells average around 7 micrometres in diameter.

name: Human sperm cell
blurb: A human sperm cell has a head and a long tail, with a total length of roughly 50 micrometres. The head carries the father's genetic material.

howWeKnow.text: Microscope measurements show a total length of about 50 to 60 micrometres, including the tail.

name: Human hair (width)
blurb: A typical human hair is about 70 micrometres across. Thickness varies from person to person and across the same person's head.

howWeKnow.text: Cross-sections of hair viewed under a microscope show diameters mostly between about 50 and 100 micrometres.

name: House dust mite
blurb: House dust mites are tiny relatives of spiders. Adults are about 0.3 millimetres long and feed on flakes of dead skin.

howWeKnow.text: Adult dust mites are measured under a microscope and are typically 0.2 to 0.3 millimetres long.

name: Grain of sand
blurb: A typical sand grain is about 0.5 millimetres across. Sand is loose rock and mineral grains between 0.06 and 2 millimetres in size.

howWeKnow.text: Sand is sorted by passing it through stacked sieves with known mesh sizes, which reveals the range of grain sizes.

name: Black garden ant (worker)
blurb: Ants are social insects, and this common black garden ant worker is about 4 millimetres long. Colonies can contain thousands of workers.

howWeKnow.text: Length is measured on preserved specimens from head to the tip of the abdomen, typically 3 to 5 millimetres for this species.

name: Human eyeball
blurb: The human eyeball is roughly a sphere about 24 millimetres across. Light enters through the cornea and is focused onto the retina.

howWeKnow.text: Ultrasound measurements of the eye's length, routinely taken in eye clinics, give about 24 millimetres in adults.

name: Human heart
blurb: An adult human heart is about 12 centimetres long and roughly the size of a fist. At rest it pumps around 5 litres of blood per minute.

howWeKnow.text: Medical imaging measures the heart's length from base to apex, which averages about 12 centimetres in adults.

name: Human brain
blurb: An adult human brain is about 16 centimetres long from front to back. Its folded surface is packed with billions of nerve cells.

howWeKnow.text: MRI scans measure the brain's maximum length from front to back, averaging about 16 centimetres in adults, though this varies between people.

name: Giraffe (height)
blurb: The tallest living land animal. An adult male giraffe stands about 5.5 metres tall, more than three times the height of a person.

howWeKnow.text: Zoologists measure wild and captive giraffes directly; adult males reach about 5 to 6 metres.

name: Blue whale
blurb: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived. Adults are typically about 25 metres long, roughly the length of two buses.

howWeKnow.instrument: Body length measurements and aerial photogrammetry
howWeKnow.text: Recorded lengths from whaling records and aerial photographs give adult averages of about 25 metres, with the largest near 30 metres.

name: Great Pyramid of Giza (base side)
blurb: Built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago, each side of its base is about 230 metres long. It was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 3,800 years.

howWeKnow.text: Modern surveys with laser and GPS instruments measure each side of the base at about 230 metres.

name: Burj Khalifa
blurb: Burj Khalifa in Dubai, completed in 2010, stands 828 metres tall, the tallest building in the world when it opened.

howWeKnow.text: The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat measures height to the top of the structure, giving 828 metres.

name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
blurb: Opened in 1932, the Sydney Harbour Bridge is about 1.15 kilometres long including its approaches. Its central steel arch spans 503 metres.

howWeKnow.text: Engineering records and surveys give a total length of 1,149 metres and an arch span of 503 metres.

name: Uluru
blurb: Uluru is a huge sandstone rock in central Australia, about 3.6 kilometres long. It rises about 348 metres above the surrounding plain.

howWeKnow.text: Survey measurements of the rock's base give a length of around 3.6 kilometres and a perimeter of about 9.4 kilometres.

name: Mount Everest
blurb: Mount Everest, on the Nepal–China border, is the highest mountain above sea level, at 8,849 metres.

howWeKnow.text: A 2020 joint survey by Nepal and China used satellite positioning to measure the summit at 8,848.86 metres above sea level.

name: Neutron star
blurb: A neutron star is the dense core left after a massive star explodes. It packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about 24 kilometres across.

howWeKnow.text: X-ray timing from telescopes such as NICER constrains neutron star radii to roughly 10 to 13 kilometres, so the diameter is about 24 kilometres.

name: Pluto
blurb: Pluto is a dwarf planet beyond Neptune, about 2,380 kilometres across. That makes it smaller than Earth's Moon.

howWeKnow.text: The New Horizons flyby in 2015 imaged Pluto and measured its diameter at about 2,377 kilometres.

name: Moon
blurb: Earth's Moon is about 3,475 kilometres across, roughly a quarter of Earth's width.

howWeKnow.text: Spacecraft and Earth-based measurements give a mean lunar diameter of about 3,474.8 kilometres.

name: Australia (east–west width)
blurb: Mainland Australia stretches about 4,000 kilometres from east to west, so a coast-to-coast drive takes days.

howWeKnow.text: Positions of the eastern and western extremes, measured on maps and satellite images, give an east–west span of about 4,000 kilometres.

name: Mars
blurb: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and about 6,800 kilometres across. Its width is roughly half that of Earth.

howWeKnow.text: Orbiters and radio tracking give Mars a mean diameter of about 6,779 kilometres.

name: Sirius B
blurb: Sirius B is a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a star, and it is about the size of Earth. It orbits the bright star Sirius A.

howWeKnow.instrument: Hubble Space Telescope imaging and stellar models
howWeKnow.text: Hubble imaging gives the orbit and mass, and white dwarf models then give a radius of about 6,000 kilometres.

name: Jupiter
blurb: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System, about 143,000 kilometres across at its equator.

howWeKnow.text: Measured by spacecraft and telescopes, Jupiter's equatorial diameter is about 142,984 kilometres.

name: Proxima Centauri
blurb: Proxima Centauri is a small red dwarf and the nearest star to the Sun. Its diameter is about 15 per cent of the Sun's.

howWeKnow.text: Stellar models estimate its radius at about 0.15 solar radii, so its diameter is roughly 15 per cent of the Sun's.

name: Earth–Moon distance
blurb: The Moon orbits Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 kilometres. Lasers bounced off mirrors left on the Moon measure this to within millimetres.

howWeKnow.text: Lasers fired from Earth reflect off retroreflectors left by Apollo missions, and timing the round trip gives the distance precisely.

name: Sirius A
blurb: Sirius A, the brightest star in the night sky, is about 1.7 times the Sun's diameter and roughly 25 times as luminous.

howWeKnow.text: Interferometry from the ground measures the angular size of Sirius A, which with its distance gives a diameter of about 2.4 million kilometres.

name: 1 astronomical unit
blurb: One astronomical unit is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres. It is now defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.

howWeKnow.text: Radar echoes and spacecraft tracking first measured this distance; since 2012 it has been fixed by definition at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.

name: Betelgeuse
blurb: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in Orion. Its diameter is roughly 760 times the Sun’s, though estimates vary because its surface pulsates.

howWeKnow.text: Interferometry resolves the star's disc, and with its distance this implies a diameter of roughly one billion kilometres.

name: Kuiper belt
blurb: The Kuiper belt is a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, spanning roughly 30 to 50 astronomical units from the Sun. Pluto is one of its best-known members.

howWeKnow.text: Surveys of distant icy bodies map where they orbit, giving a belt roughly 100 astronomical units across; its outer edge is approximate.

name: 1 light-year
blurb: One light-year is the distance light travels in one Julian year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres.

howWeKnow.instrument: Calculation from the speed of light
howWeKnow.text: It is found by multiplying the exact speed of light, 299,792,458 metres per second, by one Julian year of 31,557,600 seconds.

name: Oort cloud
blurb: The Oort cloud is a vast, hypothetical shell of icy bodies that may reach about 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun. No one has seen it directly.

howWeKnow.text: Long-period comets seem to come from a distant reservoir; its outer edge is inferred at around 100,000 AU, so the cloud is roughly 200,000 AU across.

name: Distance to Alpha Centauri
blurb: Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to the Sun, is about 4.4 light-years away. Its light takes over four years to reach us.

howWeKnow.text: The tiny yearly shift in the star's apparent position, as Earth orbits the Sun, gives a distance of about 4.37 light-years.

name: Orion Nebula
blurb: The Orion Nebula is a glowing cloud of gas and dust where new stars are forming. It is about 1,300 light-years away and visible to the naked eye.

howWeKnow.text: The cloud's apparent size in telescope images, combined with its distance, gives a width of roughly 24 light-years; estimates vary.

name: Omega Centauri
blurb: Omega Centauri is the largest known globular cluster in the Milky Way, holding millions of ancient stars. It is about 17,000 light-years away.

howWeKnow.instrument: Star count surveys and cluster modelling
howWeKnow.text: Star count surveys and cluster models give a diameter of roughly 150 light-years, though its outer edge is fuzzy.

name: Large Magellanic Cloud
blurb: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, about 160,000 light-years away. It is roughly 32,000 light-years across.

howWeKnow.text: Cepheid variable stars place the cloud about 160,000 light-years away, and its extent on the sky gives a size of roughly 32,000 light-years.

name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
blurb: The Triangulum Galaxy, also called M33, is a spiral galaxy about 2.7 million light-years away. It is one of the largest members of the Local Group.

howWeKnow.instrument: Cepheid distance and apparent sky size
howWeKnow.text: Its apparent size on the sky, combined with a distance of about 2.7 million light-years, gives a diameter of roughly 50,000 to 60,000 light-years.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
blurb: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away. It is about 220,000 light-years across.

howWeKnow.text: Cepheid variable stars place Andromeda about 2.5 million light-years away, and its apparent size then gives a diameter near 220,000 light-years.

name: Local Group
blurb: The Local Group is a cluster of more than 50 galaxies, including the Milky Way and Andromeda. It is roughly 10 million light-years across.

howWeKnow.text: Distance measurements of its member galaxies place them within a region roughly 3 megaparsecs, about 10 million light-years, across.

name: Virgo Supercluster
blurb: The Virgo Supercluster is a vast group of galaxy clusters and groups, and it contains the Local Group. It spans roughly 100 million light-years.

howWeKnow.text: Redshift surveys map where galaxies lie in three dimensions, and the supercluster's extent is estimated at around 30 megaparsecs.

name: Boötes Void
blurb: The Boötes Void is an enormous region of space containing very few galaxies. It is roughly 330 million light-years across and was found in 1981.

howWeKnow.text: Redshift measurements of galaxies around the void show it spans roughly 330 million light-years, although its edges are uncertain.

name: Laniakea
blurb: Laniakea is the vast supercluster that contains the Milky Way and our Local Group. It is about 500 million light-years across.

howWeKnow.text: Mapping how galaxies are moving across the local universe reveals a flow towards a common centre, which defines a supercluster about 500 million light-years across.

name: Sloan Great Wall
blurb: The Sloan Great Wall is one of the largest known structures in the universe, a sheet of galaxies over one billion light-years long.

howWeKnow.text: Redshift data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey trace galaxies along a wall about 1.37 billion light-years long.

name: Hubble sphere
blurb: The Hubble sphere is the distance at which galaxies recede from us at the speed of light, given today's expansion rate. Its diameter is about 28 billion light-years.

howWeKnow.text: Dividing the speed of light by the measured Hubble constant gives a radius of about 14 billion light-years, so the sphere is roughly 28 billion light-years across.
